newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy oil body says pump prices might rise further.
newsitem.headline: Italy oil body says pump prices might rise further.

text.p: Italy's oil industry body, Unione Petrolifera, said on Tuesday it could not rule out further increases to petrol prices despite criticism from Prime Minister Romano Prodi about recent pump tariff hikes.
Industry Minister Pier Luigi Bersani said the government would closely monitor the situation and hinted that the state might intervene to prevent prices climbing too steeply.

Petrol firms have been swift to push up pump costs in response to recent dollar gains, with the price of four star petrol now at a record high of 1,935 lire ($1.05) per litre and unleaded petrol at 1,840 lire a litre.

"It seems that one cannot exclude further price increases given the international situation," Unione Petrolifera's vice-chairman Domenico D'Arpizio told reporters after a hastily arranged meeting with Bersani and Prodi.
The government, worried that rising petrol prices could ignite inflation, said on Tuesday Italian pump tariffs were "without parallel" in the European Union.
"We reserve the right to evaluate the situation and see what measures need to be taken," Bersani told reporters after the emergency petrol summit.
Oil firms have lifted prices in response to dollar strength, with the U.S. currency rising by more than 20 percent against the lira since the start of the year.
Unione Petrolifera has said its members have so far have passed on only part of the added costs to their customers.
D'Arpizio blamed the high Italian prices on the domestic distribution network, which relies much less on self-service stations than elsewhere in Europe.
"This adds 40 lire a litre to the cost of Italian petrol," he told reporters.

Unione Petrolifera announced last week that member companies planned to trim Italy's vast network of retail petrol pump outlets by some 5,000 over the next two years, closing the less efficient and poorly situated stations.
Italy has over 28,000 service stations, or nearly 10 per 100 square km, the largest network in Europe.
Bersani said on Tuesday that a reform of the Italian petrol distribution system was underway. "But it is not easy," he told reporters.
